records.place: Pirque, with the Don Melchor vineyard at Puente Alto, Maipo Valley, Chile

wine.name: Don Melchor Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with small parts of Cabernet Franc, Merlot and Petit Verdot, each from parcels of its own.
wine.sites: The Don Melchor vineyard at Puente Alto, on stony alluvial ground on the north bank of the Maipo at about 650 metres, at the foot of the Andes: seven parcels of Cabernet Sauvignon, Parcel 1 among them, planted in 1979, beside smaller parcels of the other three grapes.
wine.making: Each parcel, and each smaller lot within it, is picked and fermented on its own, and the blend is chosen each year from some two hundred lots with a consultant from the Médoc. The wine is then aged about fifteen months in French oak barrels, about seven in ten of them new, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant and blackberry with red cherry, violet and rose, a note of pencil lead and the fresh mint of the Alto Maipo; fine grained, firm tannin and a long, fresh finish. Age brings cedar, coffee and dark chocolate.
wine.ageing: Tight for its first eight to ten years in a strong vintage, it then keeps and develops for a quarter of a century and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The founder's name, Melchor Concha y Toro, given to the wine with its first vintage, 1987.
The denomination of origin: the Alto Maipo area on the north bank of the river, at the foot of the Andes.
The grape named on the label, the great majority of the blend, with small parts of three others.

records.table: First made in 1987 and named for the house's founder, Don Melchor is Concha y Toro's Cabernet from stony ground at Puente Alto, at the foot of the Andes. Blackcurrant, violet and Andean mint ride on fine, firm tannin; decant it young.
records.story: Melchor Concha y Toro (1833 to 1892), a Santiago lawyer, Liberal deputy and minister of finance, founded the house in 1883 at Pirque, on land that came to him through his wife, of the Subercaseaux family. As the company tells it, he planted varieties brought from Bordeaux before phylloxera ruined the French vineyards, and a French oenologist came to oversee the first harvest. The house stayed in family hands until 1921, and its shares were listed in Santiago in 1933. Its fine wine began across the river, at Puente Alto. In 1984, by the house's account, Cabernet from its Puente Alto vineyard was taken to Bordeaux to Émile Peynaud (1912 to 2004), who saw the promise of the ground and passed the work to his collaborator in the Médoc. The first vintage, 1987, was named Don Melchor for the founder. From 1997 the vineyard was studied parcel by parcel, and each parcel has since been picked and fermented apart. In 2019 Don Melchor left the Concha y Toro range to stand as a winery of its own, Viña Don Melchor, within the group. For a sommelier, it is the eldest of the three Puente Alto Cabernets, begun nine years before Almaviva and twelve before Viñedo Chadwick.

others.name: Don Melchor DM/01
others.note: A single parcel bottling of Viña Don Melchor from Parcel 1, planted in 1979, first released with the 2022 vintage.

others.name: Casillero del Diablo

traps: Don Melchor grows at Puente Alto, across the river from the house's historic seat at Pirque, not at Pirque itself.
Almaviva is Concha y Toro's joint venture with the Mouton company, a different wine from Don Melchor though grown on the same Puente Alto ground.
Since 2019 Don Melchor has stood as its own winery, Viña Don Melchor, within the Concha y Toro group: the same wine from the same vineyard.

report: The land through the founder's wife, the Bordeaux varieties, the French oenologist at the first harvest, family hands until 1921 and the listing of 1933 rest on the company's own 20-F filing of 2019 on vinacyt.com, read in a search summary, which did not fit among the five sources.

Peynaud's dates are those the Codex's other flagship records cite from Wine Spectator's obituary; his collaborator in the Médoc and that collaborator's son, who blends Don Melchor with the house, are described rather than named.

Melchor Concha y Toro died on 21 June 1892 in the parliamentary library and 21 July in Wikipedia, so the record gives the year alone; his ministry of finance (1869 to 1870) is in Wikipedia and its mirrors.
The library calls Don Melchor Chile's first icon Cabernet; the record avoids the claim, and the house's filings call it the first ultra premium wine of the Chilean industry.

One account dates the first planting at Puente Alto to 1890 and another has Concha y Toro buying the Tocornal estate there in 1968; neither found a second source, so both are left out, as is the vineyard's size (125 or 127 hectares).
The ageing line rests on the long verticals reported by Club Oenologique (1988 to 2022) and a twenty five year tasting reported in Dallas; it is a judgement, not a measured fact.

wine.name: Almaviva
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, by far the larger part, with Carménère and Cabernet Franc, and in some vintages small parts of Petit Verdot and Merlot.
wine.sites: Puente Alto vineyards set aside for Almaviva in the Alto Maipo, on poor, stony alluvial soils that drain freely, cooled each night by cold air from the Andes.
wine.making: The grapes are cooled and left on their skins, then warmed for fermentation in stainless steel tanks sized to each parcel, with a final maceration; the malolactic follows on its own. The wine spends about ten months in the Grand Chai, then moves to a second year cellar, for sixteen to twenty months in all in French oak barrels, most of them new.
wine.glass: Cassis and black cherry over graphite and cedar, with a lift of roasted red pepper and paprika from the Carménère and a touch of dark chocolate; full and polished, with fine grained tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Approachable young for its build, it opens fully after about ten years and keeps well beyond twenty in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or more, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Count Almaviva of The Marriage of Figaro, the name written as in the playwright's own hand.
The emblem on the label: the ritual drum of the Mapuche, its design a vision of the earth and the cosmos.
The denomination of origin, the Alto Maipo area at the foot of the Andes that Almaviva shares with Don Melchor.

records.table: Concha y Toro and the Mouton Rothschild company first made Almaviva in 1996 from Puente Alto: Cabernet Sauvignon led, with Carménère adding a lift of roasted red pepper. Its label pairs a count from The Marriage of Figaro with a Mapuche drum.
records.story: The wine came before the company. Its first vintage, 1996, was made from Concha y Toro's Puente Alto vineyards under the joint direction of the Chilean house and the Bordeaux company that Baron Philippe de Rothschild (1902 to 1988) had built around Château Mouton Rothschild, which had already made Opus One in Napa with the Mondavi family. In 1997 his daughter, Baroness Philippine de Rothschild (1933 to 2014), who had succeeded him at Mouton in 1988, and the chairman of Concha y Toro signed the agreement that created Almaviva, one Franco Chilean wine from one estate. Its international launch came in 1998, and a winery designed by a Chilean architect, its roofline meant to echo the Andes, was built from that year and opened in 2000. The name and the label tell of the two cultures: Count Almaviva is a character of The Marriage of Figaro, his name written as in the playwright's own hand, and beside it stands the kultrun, the ritual drum of the Mapuche. A second wine, Epu, the Mapuche word for two, followed in later years. For a sommelier, Almaviva completes the set of French ventures abroad with Opus One in Napa and Cheval des Andes in Mendoza, and it is the one of the three that carries Carménère.

others.name: Epu
others.note: The second wine, its name the Mapuche word for two, for the two houses and cultures behind it.

traps: Almaviva's French partner is the Mouton Rothschild company; the Lafite company's Chilean estate is Los Vascos in Colchagua.
Seña is a different wine, from Aconcagua, begun by the Errázuriz family with the Mondavi winery of Napa; Almaviva is Puente Alto, in the Maipo.
Almaviva carries Carménère in its blend, which Opus One does not.

report: The library gives no founding year; the record gives 1997, the year of the partnership agreement on Almaviva's own history page, while the first vintage is 1996 (the house's wine page, the region record, and the library's quiz).
The Chilean chairman who signed in 1997 is described rather than named, his dates not looked up, and the architect of the winery is described as he may be living.

The playwright's handwriting and the kultrun rest on Bound by Wine and Lea and Sandeman's producer page, read in search summaries; Epu as the Mapuche word for two is on several merchant pages; no first vintage of Epu is given, as accounts differ (2001, 2006, 2019).

Barrel time differs by vintage in the house's sheets (16 months for 2016, 18 for 2019, 20 for 2023 with about 73 per cent new), so the making gives the range; the terroir page gives the stony alluvial soils and the cold Andean air.
That the first vintage was sold through La Place de Bordeaux in 1998 is in one account only and is left out; the playwright is not named because his dates were not looked up.
Baroness Philippine's death is 22 August 2014 on the Mouton site and 23 August in other accounts; the record gives the years only.

records.place: Alto Jahuel, Buin, Maipo Valley, Chile

wine.name: Casa Real Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon alone, from three old selections of the grape planted together in one block.
wine.sites: Carneros Viejo, a single old block at Alto Jahuel on the Andean side of the Maipo, on alluvial soils over a clay subsoil, with vines on their own roots.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel, where the first vintage, 1989, was fermented in large wooden casks. The wine is then aged in French oak barriques, most of them new, for about fourteen months in the vintages of the 2000s and eighteen to twenty months from 2018 onwards.
wine.glass: Cassis and red plum with cedar, tobacco leaf and a faint roasted green pepper; medium bodied for Maipo Cabernet, with dusty, fine tannin and fresh acidity. Old bottles turn to leather, prune and cigar box.
wine.ageing: Reserved for its first decade in a strong vintage; the house gives it twenty years and more, and the 1989 showed well when tasted at twenty four years old.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The name of the wine, the house's single block Cabernet Sauvignon, bottled apart since the 1989 vintage.
The one grape of the wine, from the Carneros Viejo block at Alto Jahuel.
The denomination of origin, Valle del Maipo in Spanish: Santiago's valley, here its Andean side at Alto Jahuel.

records.table: Santa Rita has bottled Casa Real apart since 1989: Cabernet Sauvignon from one old block, Carneros Viejo, at Alto Jahuel. Cedar, cassis and a faint roasted pepper over dusty tannin make it the old school face of Maipo Cabernet, and it ages for decades.
records.story: The house tells a story older than its vineyard. In 1814, after the patriot defeat at Rancagua, 120 soldiers of the independence army are said to have hidden at Alto Jahuel, sheltered in the Jaraquemada family's house by Paula Jaraquemada (1768 to 1851), who, the story goes, refused the royalist troops the keys; some accounts set the episode in 1818. Viña Santa Rita itself was founded on the estate in 1880 by a Santiago businessman, and from the late nineteenth century until the middle of the 1970s it was run by the family of his son in law, the García Huidobros. In 1972 the Alto Jahuel headquarters was declared a historic monument, and in 1980 the Claro group bought into the house. Its familiar 120 range is named for the soldiers of the legend. Casa Real came with the 1989 vintage: the winemakers had seen for some years what one old block of Cabernet, Carneros Viejo, could give, and that year they bottled it on its own, after the house had begun importing new French barrels in the middle of the 1980s. Decanter later named the 1989 one of its Wine Legends. For a sommelier, Casa Real is the classic Cabernet of a nineteenth century Maipo house, the counterweight to the view that Chilean quality began in the 1990s.

others.note: The house's familiar range, named for the 120 soldiers said to have hidden on the estate in 1814.

others.name: Medalla Real
others.note: The house's steady Maipo Cabernet, a step below Casa Real.

others.name: Floresta
others.note: The single vineyard range, drawn from several Chilean valleys.

Older labels and lists call it Casa Real Reserva Especial; it is the same wine, not a separate bottling.
Alto Jahuel is an area of the Maipo at Buin, not a separate valley.

report: The plan says the patriots sheltered in the cellars; the house's own reports say the Jaraquemada family home on the estate, so the record says house; Memoria Chilena ties Paula Jaraquemada's best known defiance to her hacienda at Paine and a GoChile article to 1818, so 1814 is told as the house's story with the other year beside it.

The founder, Domingo Fernández Concha, is described rather than named: his dates (1838 to 1910) were found in one account only (wein-plus); the 1980 purchase is in the house's reports and Forbes Chile, the group's founder (1934 to 2008) left unnamed.
The library names the wine Casa Real Reserva Especial; the house's sheets and recent merchants say Casa Real, so the record uses that and keeps the older name as a trap.

Barrel time: about fourteen months for 2008 and 2011 (The Wine Society), eighteen to twenty months with some 80 per cent new French oak from 2018 (Millesima, Bordeaux Index, Onshore Cellars); Decanter says up to fifteen months in a general account.
The house's Casa Real page gives Cabernet Sauvignon alone from Carneros Viejo and more than twenty years of ageing; it did not fit among the five sources.
Ungrafted vines rest on Decanter and a second account read in a search summary; the planting years of the block (the 1970s, or the 1970s and 1980s) differ, so none is given.

records.place: Macul, Peñalolén, on the edge of Santiago, Maipo Valley, Chile

wine.name: Lota
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, usually the larger part by far, with Merlot; the share moves with the vintage.
wine.sites: The old blocks of the Macul estate at the foot of the Andes, which Santiago has grown around: Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1932 and Merlot from about 1980. The importer's sheet for 2020 also names the family's Buin vineyard.
wine.making: Fermented in stainless steel tanks, with the malolactic fermentation to follow; the wine is then aged about fifteen months in French oak barriques, most of them new, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, cassis and black cherry with cedar, tobacco leaf and a touch of dark chocolate, the Merlot rounding the middle; full bodied, with ripe, firm tannin and a long, savoury finish.
wine.ageing: Firm for its first five to eight years, it keeps and gains for fifteen years and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The wine's name, shared with the coal port near Concepción where the founder made the family's fortune.
The family's name joined to that of the hacienda on the edge of Santiago it bought in 1856.
The denomination of origin, Valle del Maipo in Spanish: Santiago's own valley.

records.table: Launched in 2006 for the house's hundred and fiftieth year, Lota is Cousiño Macul's blend of old vine Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from the Macul estate, which Santiago has spread around. Dark, firm and long, it wants a decanter while young.
records.story: Matías Cousiño (1810 to 1863) made his fortune in the coal mines of Lota, on the coast near Concepción, and in 1856 he bought the Hacienda Macul at the foot of the Andes on the edge of Santiago, the year the house counts as its founding. His son and his son's wife renewed its vines in the 1860s, bringing, by the house's account, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot from Pauillac, Sauvignon from Martillac and Riesling from Alsace. In 1927, the house says, a Cabernet harvest gave rise to Antiguas Reservas, the line by which it was long known. By the 1990s Santiago had spread around the estate, and in 1996 the family bought land at Buin, further south in the Maipo, while the cellars and the old vines stayed at Macul. Lota was launched in 2006 to mark the house's hundred and fiftieth year: a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon from vines planted in 1932 and Merlot from about 1980, both from the old estate. It shares its name with the coal port where the founder's fortune began. For a sommelier, Lota is the old Santiago house's answer to the Puente Alto blends, grown on a vineyard the city has surrounded.

others.name: Antiguas Reservas Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The house's classic Maipo Cabernet, a line it dates to the Cabernet harvest of 1927.

others.name: Antiguas Reservas Chardonnay
others.note: The same line in white, from Chardonnay the house says came to the Maipo from Burgundy in the late nineteenth century.

traps: Lota is the house's old vine blend, launched in 2006; Antiguas Reservas is its classic Cabernet line, dated by the house to 1927.
Lota the wine grows at Macul in Santiago; Lota the town is the coal port near Concepción where the family's fortune was made, not a vineyard site.
Cousiño Macul's founding year is 1856, older than Santa Rita's 1880 and Concha y Toro's 1883.

report: Not in the library: each date rests on the house's own pages and a second source (Winebow's brand page and sheets, the parliamentary library of Chile, Memoria Chilena) or is hedged as the house's; 1856 is the year Matías Cousiño bought the Hacienda Macul, from which the house dates itself.

The region record's producers line names Antiguas Reservas as the house's long lived Cabernet; the plan's Lota is the wine the house presents as its flagship, launched in 2006, and the record keeps Antiguas Reservas among the others.
That Lota is named for the coal town was found only on a personal blog, not on the house's or the importer's pages, so the record says only that the wine shares its name with the town.

The son and daughter in law who renewed the vines (Luis Cousiño and Isidora Goyenechea) are described, their dates not looked up; the house dates the French cuttings to 1860 on one page and the Bordeaux journey to 1863 on another, so the record says the 1860s.
Matías Cousiño's birth is 1810 in the parliamentary library and Wikipedia, 1802 in one Memoria Chilena account; the record keeps 1810.
The Merlot's planting is 1980 or 1981 in different accounts, so the record says about 1980; one 2019 note gives 1960 for the Cabernet, against 1932 in the house's own pages and Winebow's.
Barrel time is about fifteen months, some 85 per cent new French oak, in Winebow's sheets for 2018 and 2020; Winebow's brand page says eighteen months, and the record keeps the sheets.
The Buin purchase of 1996 rests on Winebow's brand page and a Wine-Searcher note; Lota's first vintage (2003 or 2004 in different accounts) is left out.

wine.name: Viñedo Chadwick
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, alone in many vintages, with a few per cent of Petit Verdot in some since 2016, from vines planted in 2011.
wine.sites: One vineyard at Puente Alto on the north bank of the Maipo, at about 650 metres at the foot of the Andes, on stony alluvial ground where the family's polo field once lay; planted from 1992.
wine.making: Each lot is fermented in small stainless steel tanks, with concrete vats in later vintages, after a maceration of eighteen to thirty days. After the malolactic, the wine is aged about twenty two months, most of it in new French oak barrels and a share in large oak foudres.
wine.glass: Cassis, blueberry and dark cherry with liquorice, fresh mint and a touch of bitter chocolate; silky and tightly knit rather than broad, with fine, gravelly tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Firm in youth, it opens after about a decade in a strong vintage and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: Spanish for the Chadwick vineyard: the wine takes the family's name and comes from one vineyard.
The denomination of origin, Valle del Maipo in Spanish; the vineyard lies at Puente Alto, on its Andean side.

records.table: Planted in 1992 on the family's old polo field at Puente Alto, Viñedo Chadwick is the Errázuriz family's Cabernet. Its 2000 placed first at the Berlin Tasting of 2004, ahead of Château Lafite; expect cassis, mint and silky, fine tannin.
records.story: The Errázuriz house was founded in 1870 in the Aconcagua valley, north of Santiago, but its Maipo wine began as a sports ground. The family's patriarch, a keen polo player, kept a polo field at Puente Alto, and in 1992 the field was planted with Cabernet Sauvignon; the wine was named in his memory. The first vintage was 1999. On 23 January 2004, in Berlin, the family set its wines blind before thirty six European critics and writers, beside Bordeaux first growths and Tuscan reds: sixteen wines in all. Viñedo Chadwick 2000, only its second vintage, placed first and Seña 2001 second, with Château Lafite 2000 third. The result is the event most often cited for Chile's modern standing in fine wine. Petit Verdot, planted in 2011, joined the blend in small measure with the 2016 vintage, while hot years such as 2020 went back to Cabernet alone. For a sommelier, the Berlin result is the date to know: it is Chile's own blind tasting coup, held in Berlin and not in Paris, and won by a Puente Alto Cabernet from a former polo field.

others.name: Seña
others.note: The family's Aconcagua blend, begun with the Mondavi winery of Napa, which placed second at Berlin with its 2001.

others.name: Don Maximiano Founder's Reserve
others.note: The Errázuriz house's historic Aconcagua red, named for its founder.

others.name: Las Pizarras
others.note: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from schist soils on the cool Aconcagua coast.

traps: The Berlin Tasting was held in Berlin in January 2004, not in Paris and not in the 1970s; Viñedo Chadwick 2000 placed first.
Viñedo Chadwick is Puente Alto, in the Maipo; Seña, from the same family, is Aconcagua.
Don Melchor and Almaviva share the Puente Alto subzone but are Concha y Toro's wine and its venture's, not the Errázuriz family's.

cards.front: Viñedo Chadwick: what was the vineyard before it was planted in 1992?
cards.back: The family's polo field at Puente Alto, kept by the patriarch, a keen polo player, in whose memory the wine is named.

cards.front: Which grape is Viñedo Chadwick, and what joined it in small measure from 2016?
cards.back: Cabernet Sauvignon, alone in many vintages; a few per cent of Petit Verdot, planted in 2011, in some years since.

report: The library's founded year, 1999, is the first vintage; the vines were planted on the polo field in 1992 (The Drinks Business, Decanter, Vinous), and the field itself is older.

The patriarch is described rather than named: one source dates him 1929 to 1996 and another implies he died in 1993, so his dates stand unconfirmed; that he helped found a polo club in Santiago is in one account only and is left out.

Lafite 2000 in third place is in Decanter's report and two other accounts (Académie du Vin, a Canadian magazine); the lower placings differ between lists and are left out, as is the later run of the tasting in other cities.

The making rests on the importers' sheets (Hatch Mansfield for 2013 to 2015, Mark Anthony for 2020): about twenty two months, 73 to 80 per cent new French oak, with Stockinger foudres from 2013; the Petit Verdot and the all Cabernet 2020 are on the estate's own past vintages page.
